summary: High-performing space thumbnails rely on a single enormous visual mystery, a recognizable subject, and very short high-contrast text. The strongest concepts frame NASA, national space programs, planets, spacecraft, or unexplained cosmic objects as revelations, anomalies, failures, or urgent discoveries. Cinematic lighting, stark black space, warm-versus-cool contrast, isolated subjects, borders, and occasional archival or breaking-news cues reinforce credibility and urgency.
viralPatterns: Official discovery framing: NASA, China, the Soviets, or astronomers found something unexpected.
Anomaly language: strange, impossible, horrifying, seriously off, wild, or not what you think.
Recognizable subject plus hidden truth: a planet, moon, spacecraft, mission, or cosmic object is shown in an unfamiliar way.
Concrete mystery objects: unusual formations, blurry discoveries, probes, rovers, habitats, cutaways, and unexplained signals.
Future-construction promises: how NASA or SpaceX will build cities, bases, habitats, or engines.
Historical secrecy and declassification: Soviet missions, nuclear tests, archival probes, and recovered evidence.
Urgent news packaging: NASA LIVE, breaking-news styling, red circles, warning colors, and implied institutional panic.
Extreme scale contrast: tiny spacecraft or humans against giant planets, explosions, habitats, or cosmic structures.
Simple visual questions: one central object and one unresolved claim that can be understood instantly at small size.
Repeated brand consistency: thin white borders, lower-left channel branding, oversized uppercase text, and cinematic grading.
Cutaway reveals: visible spacecraft interiors, lunar bases, rooms, machinery, astronauts, or hidden engineering.
High emotional stakes: danger, failure, horror, impossible discoveries, and implications for humanity.
thumbnailFormats: Cinematic planetary reveal: giant planet or moon landscape, dark star field, centered uppercase claim, and warm atmospheric lighting.
Cosmic void reveal: curved glowing cosmic edge on one side, empty black space on the other, and one unsettling word or answer.
Monochrome anomaly reveal: hazy yellow, gray, or red surface with one ambiguous feature and a blunt phrase such as THIS IS STRANGE.
Dramatic formation reveal: one towering volcano, plume, structure, or silhouette isolated against a sparse planetary landscape.
Cosmic horror object: uncanny eye, mechanical sphere, organic structure, or impossible planet with extreme blue-orange contrast.
Breaking-news mystery: spacecraft or NASA identifier beside a blurry object, divider line, red circle, alert banner, and urgent text.
Archival artifact mystery: Soviet or NASA probe on alien terrain with distressed monochrome treatment and classified-document styling.
Space blast archival: centered nuclear explosion or energetic event in black space with film border and declassified cues.
Lunar blueprint reveal: habitat or base centered on the Moon, Earth visible as a scale reference, and NASA'S PLAN headline.
Cutaway spacecraft reveal: full-width vehicle cross-section exposing rooms, machinery, seats, astronauts, or glowing engines.
Mission failure scene: recognizable capsule or rocket with workers, recovery equipment, warning colors, and a short negative claim.
Pixelated cosmic question: ambiguous red-orange object, dark blocky background, directional arrow, and a provocative question.
titleFormulas: Real Images of [Object] Show That Something Is Seriously Off
This Is What [Planet/Mission] REALLY Looks Like
What Is Actually Happening With [Current Space Object]
NASA Just Confirmed [Mission/Object] Found Something Impossible
What Life Inside [Spacecraft] Will Be Like
What Happened When [Country] [Extreme Action] in Space
The First Real Images of [Planet/Object] - What We Found?
A [Scale/Distance] So Huge Your Brain Can't Comprehend It
doList: Use one dominant subject that remains identifiable at mobile thumbnail size.
Pair a familiar name such as NASA, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, SpaceX, or Voyager with an unfamiliar visual claim.
Keep thumbnail copy to two to five large uppercase words and make it readable without the title.
Use a clear emotional promise: anomaly, danger, secrecy, failure, discovery, or future transformation.
Create strong separation with black space, bright subject lighting, and warm-versus-cool color contrast.
Use arrows, circles, dividers, or alert labels only when they direct attention to a genuinely ambiguous feature.
Show concrete evidence or an object tied to the title: probe, rover, capsule, terrain, habitat, explosion, or cosmic image.
Use cutaways and scale references such as astronauts, Earth, workers, or spacecraft to explain complex concepts instantly.
Reserve borders and lower-left branding for consistent channel recognition without obscuring the focal subject.
Test every concept at small size for one-second comprehension and a clear unanswered question.
Match the visual promise to the video so the mystery is resolved with evidence rather than generic spectacle.
dontList: Do not fill the frame with several competing planets, objects, or text blocks.
Do not rely on vague space imagery that lacks a recognizable subject or specific mystery.
Do not make the headline repeat the title without adding a visual claim or emotional tension.
Do not use tiny text, long sentences, or low-contrast lettering that disappears on mobile.
Do not obscure the main object with oversized logos, decorative borders, or excessive labels.
Do not use red circles, arrows, breaking-news graphics, or NASA branding as empty decoration.
Do not present CGI as real imagery unless the thumbnail clearly supports a documentary or simulation context.
Do not overuse identical planet compositions without changing the anomaly, object, or visual story.
Do not make a planet or spacecraft so dark, hazy, or cropped that viewers cannot identify it.
Do not promise impossible discoveries, panic, or hidden evidence unless the video can substantiate the claim.
Do not crowd cutaway scenes with unreadable interiors or figures that collapse into visual noise.
Do not use generic fear language when a concrete formation, mission event, or discovery can carry the curiosity.

visualLessons.title: What Is Beyond Edge Of The Universe?
visualLessons.subject: A large glowing circular field filled with stars and galaxies on the left, set against a black background
visualLessons.composition: The left two-thirds contain the curved edge of a blue cosmic sphere densely packed with stars; the right side is mostly empty black space with centered white text
visualLessons.colors: Deep navy and black with electric blue-violet edges, white stars, and small warm white and orange highlights
visualLessons.emotionalHook: The sharp contrast between a richly detailed universe and the stark word "NOTHING" creates a visually surprising contradiction
visualLessons.whyItWorks: The thumbnail uses a simple split composition, high-contrast text, and a dramatic claim that reduces an enormous cosmic question to one unsettling answer

visualLessons.title: Jupiter Is Not What You Think
visualLessons.subject: A massive swirling Jupiter-like gas planet with layered cloud bands, a bright storm formation, glowing atmospheric regions, stars, and the Milky Way
visualLessons.composition: The planet fills the lower and middle frame, with a towering cloud formation on the left and a bright glowing atmospheric edge on the lower right. Large text spans the upper center. A small channel logo sits in the lower left, and a thin white rectangular border frames the image.
visualLessons.colors: Warm sepia, copper, bronze, and cream tones across the planet and clouds, contrasted with a nearly black star field and cool white text and border
visualLessons.emotionalHook: The enormous distorted planet and dramatic storm structure create visual uncertainty, while the bold statement challenges the viewer's assumption about what Jupiter looks like.
visualLessons.whyItWorks: The thumbnail combines a recognizable subject with an unfamiliar, highly dramatic transformation. Strong warm contrast, a giant centered planet, oversized readable text, and a framed cinematic layout make the image easy to scan and suggest a surprising hidden truth.
